turns.doctor_question: Hi, welcome. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi. Yeah, thanks. Well, um, it’s... it’s honestly my job that’s the main issue right now, which is why I finally made this appointment. I’m a jeweler—I do a lot of custom metalwork, stone setting, resizing, that kind of thing. And usually, I love it. I can just sit at my bench with my loupe on and just, you know, zone in on the metal for hours. You have to be incredibly precise when you're working with gold and precious stones, obviously, because one slip of a file and you've ruined a piece. 

But lately, what really brought me in is that my mind just won’t stay on one thing anymore. It’s like a pinball machine. I’ll be sitting right there at the bench, and I’m looking at this tiny saw mark on a ring that I need to buff out, but before I even pick up the tool, I’m suddenly thinking about a customer email I need to answer. So I go to check that, but then there's a noise outside—like a truck backing up or just someone talking on the sidewalk—and I'm completely focused on that instead. And then I turn back around, and I realize I’ve completely lost the whole work order. Like, the actual paper ticket with the client's details is just gone, buried somewhere, and I have no idea what step I was even on. It’s just jumping from the metal, to the computer, to the window, all day long, and I just can't seem to rein my attention in to actually finish a single piece of jewelry.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly states they cannot rein their attention in to finish a single piece of jewelry, indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient describes losing the physical work order ticket necessary for their job.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as a truck backing up or people talking outside.
symptom_reasoning.S039: The patient describes their mind jumping like a pinball machine between tasks and being easily drawn to irrelevant external noises, matching manic distractibility and frequent task switching.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have trouble paying attention as a child?
turns.patient_response:
No, honestly... that’s the thing that’s so weird about all this. When I was a kid? Not at all. I was actually the exact opposite. I could sit for hours and just lock in. 

I remember when I was maybe, I don't know, ten or eleven, my grandpa gave me this old wooden cigar box full of broken watches and pocket clocks. Just absolute junk, really, but I took them all apart piece by piece on the living room rug. I would sit there for literally half the day, just organizing the tiny gears and screws into little piles. My mom would have to practically yell at me to come into the kitchen to eat dinner because I was just so completely absorbed in it. I wouldn't even hear her the first three times she called. 

And school was the same way, really. I mean, I wasn’t some academic genius—I just got my high school diploma and went straight into an apprenticeship to learn metalworking—but I never had teachers calling home saying I was daydreaming or bouncing off the walls or anything like that. I’d just sit quietly, usually sketching designs in the margins of my notebooks or just doing the work. I was always good with my hands and always hyper-focused on whatever little project I had right in front of me. 

So this whole... brain jumping around thing? It’s completely new. It’s not like I was one of those kids who couldn't sit still or needed extra help paying attention. It’s just happening *now*, which is why it’s so incredibly frustrating for me. Because I *know* what it feels like to focus. I used to be the most focused person in the room, and now it's like that part of my brain just suddenly forgot how to do the one thing I've always been best at.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t an immediate problem in front of you?
turns.patient_response:
Worrying? No, not really. I mean, obviously if a client is mad about a custom piece being late, I’ll stress about that specific thing, but just sitting around worrying about nothing? No, that’s never really been my personality. 

My mom, now, she’s a huge worrier. She’ll call me up on a Tuesday morning and ask if I’ve checked the air pressure in my tires because she read some article on Facebook about blowouts on the highway, and I’m just like, "Mom, I drive two miles to the shop at thirty miles an hour, I think I'm fine." But me? I don’t do that. I actually think working with metal for so long kind of trains you out of worrying about things that haven't happened yet. Because when you're soldering a joint on a gold ring, right? You have the torch in your hand, the flame is right there, and if you worry about melting the gold, your hand shakes. And if your hand shakes, you move the heat to the wrong spot and you actually *do* melt the gold and ruin hours of work. So you just have to be completely in the moment. If a problem happens—like a stone chips or a bezel tears—you just fix it right then and there. You don't sit around beforehand agonizing over whether the stone *might* chip. 

So, yeah, no, I don't really have that floating worry or whatever you want to call it. My brain is definitely jumping all over the place right now, like I was saying before with the ticket orders and the window and all that, but it's not because I'm scared or stressed about some imaginary problem. It's just... fast. My mind is just moving way too fast. But I'm definitely not sitting around worrying.

symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient describes their brain as 'jumping all over the place' and states that their mind is 'moving way too fast', indicating racing thoughts.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies experiencing generalized or floating worry, stating they do not sit around worrying about things that haven't happened.

turns.doctor_question: Have you needed much less sleep than usual lately and still felt full of energy?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, actually, that’s exactly what was happening for a while there. It was the craziest thing. I would go to bed at, I don't know, maybe midnight or one in the morning, and then my eyes would just snap open at like three a.m. So I was sleeping maybe two or three hours, tops. 

But the weird part is, I wouldn't even be groggy. You know how usually if you wake up in the middle of the night, you feel like you've been hit by a truck and you can barely keep your eyes open? Not me. I would wake up completely clear-headed. Like, crystal clear. And I’d just feel this huge surge of energy, just so incredibly excited to get to work. I'd jump right out of bed and head straight for my workbench to start cutting stones. I had this batch of rough Ethiopian opals and some really nice turquoise that I was just dying to shape, and I couldn't even wait for normal business hours to start. 

Or if I wasn't cutting stones, I’d be on my phone, snapping pictures and posting all these new design concepts and wax carvings to my shop's social media pages way before sunrise. It was actually kind of amazing, honestly, because normally I need a solid eight hours or my hands get shaky, which is an absolute disaster when you're trying to set tiny stones. But during this stretch? Two or three hours of sleep and boom, I’m up, I’m wired, I don't even need a single drop of coffee. 

My roommate would come out to the kitchen for a glass of water at four in the morning and I’m already fully dressed, polishing a silver pendant and just totally in the zone. I just felt like I had an endless tank of gas, you know? Like my body just suddenly decided that sleep was a waste of time and I could just keep creating and working without ever really needing to shut down to rest. It felt great at the time, to be honest, just getting so much done before the sun even came up.

symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient reports a 'huge surge of energy,' feeling 'wired,' and having an 'endless tank of gas.'

turns.doctor_question: During that period, did you feel unusually euphoric or on top of the world?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, actually, "lit up" is exactly how I would describe it. It was... I don't even know how to explain it properly, but it was like I was vibrating on a completely different frequency than everyone else. 

There was this one weekend, right in the middle of all this, where I had a booth at this local artisan craft show. Usually, those things are exhausting. You're standing on concrete all day, smiling at people who just want to look and never buy anything, but this time? This time I felt absolutely invincible. I was talking to everyone, making connections, selling pieces I thought would sit in my display case for months. By the time the show ended, I felt larger than life. Like, I was packing up my velvet trays and I just felt this rushing, glowing sensation in my chest, like I was the most talented jeweler in the entire state and everyone was finally waking up to it. I felt like I could have walked out of that convention center and started my own international brand right then and there. 

But the flip side of that—and this is where it got really messy—was that if anyone tried to pop that bubble, I just lost it. I mean, completely snapped. My buddy who runs the leather stall next to mine at the weekend market, he came over while I was packing up and said something like, "Hey man, you look exhausted, you should take Monday off and just sleep." And I just... I laid into him. I told him he was lazy, that he didn't understand what real drive looked like, that he was trying to hold me back because he was jealous of how much I sold. I was just so incredibly irritable. 

And it wasn't just him. If anyone—my roommate, my clients, anyone—asked me to stick to normal shop hours or suggested I slow down and maybe not work on a custom silver cuff at three in the morning with a loud polishing wheel, I would just bite their head off. I felt so amazing, so full of this bright, buzzing energy, and I just couldn't stand the idea that these... these regular, slow-moving people were trying to drag me back down to their level. It was like going from feeling like a literal god to just pure, snapping anger in the span of two seconds, all because someone asked me a simple question about slowing down.
